- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate; reduce forecast slightly, especially after spikes.
- When sentiment is negative or mixed (≤0.33), model often underestimates; increase forecast gently, especially if recent prices are falling.
- Model frequently overshoots after sharp upward moves (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days), especially if sentiment was bullish; apply a “cool-down” correction by subtracting 1–3% from peak forecast.
- If sentiment shifts from bullish to bearish mid-horizon, model often fails to adjust; apply a “sentiment pivot” rule: reduce forecast by 1–2% per day of negative sentiment accumulation.
- Mean reversion bias: if forecast is >10% above recent 5-day average, reduce by 0.5–1.5% per day until convergence; if below, increase by 0.5–1.5% per day.
- Horizon-specific: 30-day forecasts often overreact to short-term sentiment; apply a “lagged sentiment filter” — weight recent sentiment (last 3–5 days) more heavily than distant sentiment for 30d forecasts.
- If sentiment is neutral or volatile (0.33–0.67), model tends to err on the side of overconfidence; apply a “volatility dampener” — reduce forecast by 0.5–1.0% for each day of high volatility (e.g., >1.5% daily range).
